rv.q: Those blocks have assumed a towering, powerful shape by the end of “Mecca” that speaks to mortal hopes and fears so directly it makes you catch your breath.
Rosemary Harris gives a performance of such fierce intelligence and emotional complexity that she transforms what could have been a talky three-character play into a riveting theatrical experience.
By the time Harris delivers Miss Helen's final speech about her quixotic artistic quest, you may find yourself reaching for a tissue rather than your cellphone.
Theatre Company's somewhat sleepy but still satisfying production of "The Road to Mecca" opened Tuesday at the Theater featuring Carla Gugino, Jim Dale and the luminous Rosemary Harris.
But a compelling case is made for this wordy 1984 drama about individual and artistic freedom only deep into its second act.
Alas, in Gordon Edelstein's cautious, small-scaled staging in the large Theatre, such complex intimacies strain to be heard, much less understood.
Everyone and everything feels too far apart in this Mecca; actors can’t seem to get a firm grip on one another and nothing ever feels the least bit urgent.
Harris is riveting, even when sitting still and absorbing the other two characters' thoughts.
Harris, still luminous at 84 years old, caps a brilliant career with a deeply felt performance.
Her delicate and detailed performance of a woman battling the darkness that can seep into one's soul shimmers with its own bright light.
It works sometimes, yet there is a sense that the play traverses the same ground over and over again.

Despite sterling performances from Carla Gugino, Jim Dale, and the luminous Rosemary Harris, it's a bit of a slog to 'Mecca' as the show tries to punch its way across the footlights in the Roundabout Theatre Company's too-large Theatre.

Harris is a luminous and appealing Helen, and Dale gives a wisely subdued, nuanced portrayal of Marius. Gugino is a bit overstated at times as Elsa, but she also gives the play a welcome jolt of energy.
Yet this Road to Mecca, at the Theatre through March 4, is long, winding, and, in the end, more than a little unsatisfying.
Although the production features a fine cast including Rosemary Harris, Jim Dale and Carla Gugino, it's about as exciting overall as watching paint dry.
Harris is a transcendent, complex Helen, subtly displaying her strengths, weaknesses and insecurities.

cn.t: Harris shines in this wordy, slow-paced Fugard drama, but critics find the production a tedious journey. The intimate three-hander struggles in the oversized venue, though patient viewers are rewarded by luminous performances.
